Q: std::cos produces different results in GCC and MSVC A:

Accuracy of floating point operations is standardized this way: https://eel.is/c++draft/basic.fundamental#12

Except as specified in [basic.extended.fp], the object and value representations and accuracy of operations of floating-point types are implementation-defined.

(emphasis mine).

Unfortunately, I see no way to enforce that different implementations give the same results.

STerliakov link is interesting in this regard, in order to get more insights. And also an academic reference and the most recent version to this day (thanks to Martin Brown).

As commented by Jesper Juhl, when dealing with floating point operations, consider that there are no such thing as strict equality: give you an expected acceptable relative or absolute error, which depend on your exact application.

IMHO a max "reasonable" error should have been defined to allow for numericians ro reason about accuracy within there codes, but it does not seem to be the case.

Q: C# vs C++. Which is Better? A:

There is no "better". There's only "better for some specific purpose". So, what are you doing and why do you think one language might be better than another?

Q: How to get fork join/join_any to work with a loop A:

If you want to wait for all of the processes fork'ed by the fork-jone_none to complete, you put a wait fork; statement after the for loop. The wait fork statements waits for all child processes of the current thread to complete.

If there are processes created by a fork-jone_none before this for loop is still active and you don’t want to wait for them to finish, you need to put this piece of code in an isolation thread.

fork
  some_other_process;
join_none
fork 
  begin : isolation_process
    for(int j=1; j <=3; ++j) begin : for_loop
      fork
         automatic int k = j;
         begin
            .... # use k here
         end
      join_none
    end : for_loop
  wait fork; // will not wait for some other process
 end :isolation_thread
 join

To get the behavior of the fork-join_any requires some handshaking signal or event in each process to signal that it is done.

event join_any_event;
for(int j=1; j <=3; ++j) begin : for_loop
      fork
         automatic int k = j;
         begin
            .... # use k here
            ->> join_any_event;
         end
      join_none
    end : for_loop
  @join_any_event;

Q: How to get the p values from LSD.test in R? A:

Assuming you are using the agricolae library, if you want the p-values for each of the contrasts, you'll need to set group=FALSE when running the test and then extract the comparison table

result <- LSD.test(linmod, trt = 'trt', group=FALSE)
result$comparison
#                  difference pvalue signif.        LCL      UCL
# control - pink    3.1666667 0.0031      **  1.1286894 5.204644
# control - yellow  2.8333333 0.0075      **  0.7953561 4.871311
# pink - yellow    -0.3333333 0.7434         -2.3713106 1.704644

Q: Docker Desktop always switches or create to 'desktop-linux' context on launch A:

There is no such thing as Docker Desktop using the default context. Docker Desktop can only run using its own virtual machine engine, which you're seeing as:

unix:///home/username/.docker/desktop/docker.sock

Q: Unexpected character 'I' when displaying union value A:

SystemVerilog does not guarantee the alignment of bits between different members of an unpacked union unless they have the same type. You are defining an unpacked union.

Unpacked unions in SystemVerilog have limited utility unless interfaced with C via the DPI. Many tools lack support for them, which likely explains the bug you’re seeing.

FYI, SystemVerilog 1800-2023 introduced a feature that allows for soft packed unions, which can have members with varying bit widths and are right-justified. Prior to this version, all union members had to have the same bit width.
